person.name: Abigail_Adams
person.tagline: Letters from the Revolutionary Home Front
person.summary: Abigail Adams was an American political advisor and letter writer whose correspondence with John Adams records the Revolutionary era and the early United States. She managed her family’s household and finances during long separations, urged greater legal consideration for women, and served as the wife of the nation’s second president.

conclusion: Abigail Adams's letters with John Adams remain major records of political debate, family life, and civilian experience during the American Revolution and the early republic. Her appeal that lawmakers remember women remains widely quoted in studies of women's legal and political history. Editors, historians, and readers continue to use the Adams family correspondence to study the founding era.

events.title: Birth in Weymouth
events.description: Abigail Smith was born in Weymouth, Massachusetts, to William Smith and Elizabeth Quincy Smith. William Smith was a liberal [[Congregational minister|Congregational minister]] in the North Parish. The Smiths had three daughters and a son, and Abigail was their second child.

images.caption: Abigail Adams birthplace in Weymouth, Massachusetts
images.creator: John Phelan

Congregational minister.explanation: A Congregational minister led a Protestant church governed by its local congregation. William Smith belonged to a liberal New England religious tradition that emphasized reason and morality in addition to faith.

events.title: Educates Herself at Home
events.description: Frequent childhood illness prevented Abigail Smith from attending formal school in Weymouth, Massachusetts. Her mother, Elizabeth Smith, taught her and her sisters to read, write, and do arithmetic, while the family libraries gave Abigail access to English and French literature.
events.background:
The Smith household gave Abigail access to the large libraries of her father, uncle, and grandfather. Her grandmother, Elizabeth Quincy, also contributed to her education. As she grew older, she read with friends to continue her learning.

In later life, Abigail considered herself deprived of an education because girls rarely received formal educational opportunities. She came to be regarded as one of the most erudite women to serve as first lady.

events.title: Meets John Adams
events.description: In 1759, fifteen-year-old Abigail Smith met John Adams when he visited her family’s household in Weymouth, Massachusetts, with his friend Richard Cranch. Cranch was courting Abigail’s older sister, Mary Smith, bringing John and Abigail into one another’s social circle.

events.title: Marries John Adams
events.description: On October 25, 1764, Abigail Smith married John Adams at her parents' home in Weymouth, Massachusetts. Her father, William Smith, conducted the ceremony. Afterward, the couple rode to John Adams's inherited farm in Braintree, Massachusetts, to begin their household.

events.title: Returns to Braintree Farm
events.description: In 1774, Abigail Adams returned with her children from Boston to the family farm in Braintree, Massachusetts, as growing political unrest made Boston increasingly unstable. John Adams traveled to Philadelphia for the Continental Congress, leaving Abigail responsible for the household, farm, and children.

images.caption: John Adams homestead in Braintree, Massachusetts
images.creator: Unknown authorUnknown author

events.title: Urges Women's Legal Rights
events.description: On March 31, 1776, Abigail Adams wrote from Braintree, Massachusetts, to John Adams, a delegate in Philadelphia's [[Continental Congress|Continental Congress]]. She urged him to remember women when new laws were drafted and warned against giving husbands unlimited legal power.

images.caption: Abigail Adams letter concerning women's rights
images.creator: Skloewer

Continental Congress.explanation: The Continental Congress was the revolutionary governing body in which delegates from the American colonies coordinated resistance to British rule and debated the new nation's laws and government.

events.background:
Adams's request formed part of her sustained argument that women had minds equal to men's and should be educated. She believed women could use their intellectual abilities to guide their children and husbands. Her warning included a threat that women would “foment a Rebellion” against laws made without their voice or representation.

John Adams called her proposal an “extraordinary code of laws.” He wrote that men had only “the name of masters.” He joked that giving up that title would subject men to the “despotism of the petticoat.”

events.title: Invests Wartime Savings
events.description: In 1777, Abigail Adams invested funds through her uncle Cotton Tufts in debt instruments issued to finance the Revolutionary War. She managed these investments while overseeing the Adams farm and household in Braintree, Massachusetts.

images.caption: Continental Congress broadside issued in 1777
images.creator: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress

events.title: Joins Family in Paris
events.description: In 1784, Abigail Adams left Braintree, Massachusetts, and crossed the Atlantic by ship with her daughter Abigail Adams Smith, known as Nabby. They traveled to Paris to join John Adams, who held an American diplomatic post there, and John Quincy Adams. After arriving, Abigail took charge of a large household with servants.
events.background:
She had feared the long sea crossing before she left, but found the voyage interesting. Paris initially brought a different difficulty. Running a large home with a retinue of servants was unfamiliar work, and she felt overwhelmed by it.

In the months that followed, she made numerous friends and grew fond of the theater and opera. Parisian women’s fashions fascinated her. She also wrote ruefully that she would never be in the fashion herself.

background_images.caption: Satire of the fashionable Parisian crowd shopping and walking under the arcade of the Palais Royal. 1787 Colour aquatint

events.title: Moves to London
events.description: Congress appointed John Adams the first United States minister to [[Court of St James's|the British royal court]]. In 1785, Abigail traveled from Paris to London with John Adams and their daughter Nabby. In London, she temporarily cared for Thomas Jefferson's daughter Mary, whom the family called Polly.

Court of St James's.explanation: The Court of St James's is the formal name for the British royal court and the diplomatic designation used for foreign missions to Britain.

events.title: Returns to Peacefield
events.description: In 1788, Abigail and John Adams traveled by sea from London to Quincy, Massachusetts, after completing their diplomatic assignments in Europe. They returned to Peacefield, the Adams family home, where Abigail directed its enlargement and remodeling as the family resumed life in Massachusetts.

Peacefield.explanation: Peacefield, also called the Old House, was the Adams family's home in Quincy. Abigail and John returned there in 1788, and the house remains part of Adams National Historical Park.

events.title: Cares for Susanna in Massachusetts
events.description: John Adams became the second president of the United States in Philadelphia on March 4, 1797. Abigail remained in Massachusetts to care for Susanna Boylston Adams, John's dying mother. She did not attend the inauguration.

events.title: Shelters Her Granddaughter
events.description: In 1800, Abigail Adams brought her three-year-old granddaughter Susanna, Charles Adams's daughter, to the President's House in Philadelphia. Charles died shortly afterward. Abigail also housed children of her brother William Smith and her brother-in-law John Shaw, who struggled with alcoholism.

images.caption: President's House in Philadelphia
images.creator: William L. Breton, artist and lithographer.

events.title: Moves into the White House
events.description: In November 1800, Abigail Adams moved into the unfinished President’s House in Washington, D.C., with her husband, President John Adams. She found the setting beautiful but struggled to maintain the distant mansion and used the East Room to dry the family’s laundry.

images.caption: The White House in Washington, D.C.
images.creator: www.GlynLowe.com from Hamburg, Germany

events.title: Renews Jefferson Correspondence
events.description: In 1812, Abigail Adams supported John Adams’s renewal of his correspondence with Thomas Jefferson after years of political estrangement. John Adams began the exchange with a New Year’s letter, and the correspondence continued while Abigail remained at Peacefield in Quincy, Massachusetts.

events.title: Loses Daughter Nabby
events.description: On August 15, 1813, Abigail Adams's daughter Abigail Adams Smith, known as Nabby, died at the family home in Quincy, Massachusetts, after three years of severe pain from breast cancer. Nabby had returned from her farm in New York to die at her parents' home, where Abigail cared for her.

events.title: Death at Peacefield
events.description: Abigail Adams spent her final years ill at Peacefield, her home in Quincy. She died there of [[typhoid fever|typhoid fever]] on October 28, 1818. John Adams was with her when she told him that she was ready to go.

typhoid fever.explanation: Typhoid fever is a bacterial infection that can cause prolonged fever and severe illness. In the 19th century, it often spread through contaminated food or water and had no modern antibiotic treatment.

event_class.place_of_rest: United First Parish Church, Quincy, Massachusetts
